newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends near session highs in US after payrolls.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends near session highs in US after payrolls.

text.p: The dollar ended an eventful week on a positive note, closing higher against the yen and the mark on Friday after the release of U.S. payrolls data and comments from Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin.
The U.S. Labor Department's much-anticipated March employment report showed that a modest 175,000 jobs were added to the U.S. economy in March -- below Wall Street consensus forecasts.

But the data also showed a further decline in the unemployment rate to 5.2 percent and sizable wage gains -- both worrisome inflation signs and signals that Fed policymakers could follow up last week's interest rate hike with another in May.

"I don't think it was the payrolls number so much as it was the wages," said John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank. "That's something that the Fed said they would monitor closely and when that showed an increase, expectations of higher rates drove the dollar up."

Average hourly earnings rose by five cents for the second consecutive month in March -- from $12.10 to $12.15. Over the past year, the report showed that hourly wages have risen 4.0 percent, the biggest rise since the 12 months ended June 1990.
The dollar ended the day at 124.27/32 yen, up from 123.93/03 at the open and 122.59/64 on Thursday.
Against the mark, the dollar broke through key resistance at 1.6850 late in the session, to end at 1.6860/65, up from 1.6762/67 in early trade.

The dollar performed admirably in the face of more volatility in U.S. asset markets on Friday. The Dow industrials slumped after the payrolls report and traded in the minus column for much of the session, before popping higher in the late afternoon to close up 49 points at 6526.
The yield of the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond pushed up to a seven-month high of 7.14 percent on Friday, before the T-bond recouped some of its losses in late trade.

"We're not really following the asset markets and instead seeing more interest to buy the dollar on the interest rate outlook," said Lizbeth Goldberg, assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank.
The dollar was helped late in the day by comments from Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, who said in a speech that the strong dollar was clearly helping keep U.S. inflation subdued.

These comments, when taken together with U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's overnight remarks in Japan, suggested to some traders that U.S. officials are content with the dollar at its current strong levels.

Rubin, in Japan on his way to a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines, rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency -- and thus a weaker U.S. dollar -- was the best way to avoid a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus with the United States.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," Rubin told reporters.
His remarks reassured investors who had feared that harsher rhetoric over Japan's burgeoning bilateral trade surplus would pressure the dollar.
In other trade on Friday, the dollar pushed up to a fresh two-year high against the Canadian dollar before ending at C$1.3915/20 against C$1.3902/07 at the open.
The dollar settled at 1.4426/31 Swiss francs against 1.4355/65 in early trade, while the British pound shrank to $1.6340/45 after opening at $1.6385/95.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7755/60, down from $0.7773/78.
